summary: Defines the Layer 3 VPN Network Model, a YANG model a network controller can use to provision L3VPN services inside a service provider network. It complements the customer-facing Layer 3 VPN Service Model and gives a network-centric view. The controller uses it to derive device configuration.

eli5.summary: The customer says what service they want. This describes the detailed plan the network uses to build it.

questions: what is a vpn node in l3nm
subtitle: A YANG model that gives a network controller a network-side view of a Layer 3 VPN, below the customer-facing service model.

tldr.problem: The Layer 3 VPN Service Model (L3SM) describes a VPN from the customer's point of view and hides the provider network, so it is too abstract for a controller that must build the service and coordinate things like route targets and route distinguishers.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9182 defines the L3VPN Network Model (L3NM), a YANG module called ietf-l3vpn-ntw. It describes each VPN service as VPN nodes (typically one per provider edge router) with network accesses, CE-PE routing, QoS, security and multicast settings, reusing the common module from RFC 9181.
tldr.outcome: A service orchestrator can use it to ask a network controller for a VPN, and a controller can derive device configuration from it. It does not replace the L3SM, and how it maps to device configuration is left to implementations.

facts.value: static, BGP, OSPF, IS-IS, RIP, VRRP

today: RFC 9182 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2022 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It complements, and does not obsolete, the L3SM in RFC 8299, and it builds on the common module in RFC 9181.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
The L3SM (RFC 8299) describes the customer view of a Layer 3 VPN and is limited to the role of a customer service model. RFC 9182 defines a L3VPN Network Model (L3NM) that gives a network-centric view instead. It can carry network-specific information between a service orchestrator and a network controller or orchestrator, and it enables capabilities such as resource management or a multi-domain interface where logical resources like route targets and route distinguishers must be coordinated.

The document does not obsolete the L3SM; the two have similar goals but different scopes and views. The L3NM started from a prune-and-extend approach based on the L3SM but is not an augment of it, because network needs call for a different structure. It uses the common VPN module in RFC 9181 and conforms to the Network Management Datastore Architecture.

It targets Layer 3 VPNs based on BGP provider edges (RFC 4364) and multicast VPNs. It does not try to cover deployments where connectivity is built by coordinating different VPNs in different underlying networks.
sections.eli5: The old model was the customer's order form. This one is the provider's internal work order, written for the machines that build the network.

sections.title: Reference Architecture
sections.content:
The L3NM architecture expands the one in RFC 8299 by splitting orchestration into three parts: service orchestration, network orchestration and domain orchestration. The RFC advocates a clear separation between service and network orchestration for flexibility, with a dedicated interface between them that carries network information hidden from customers. Translating customer-facing information into network-centric information, and back, is implementation specific.

Following RFC 8309, four model levels are shown: the customer service model (for example l3vpn-svc), the service delivery model (l3vpn-ntw), the network configuration model and the device configuration model. The customer may request a service with the L3SM or with more abstract models, such as an IP Connectivity Provisioning Profile, an enhanced VPN (VPN+) service or an IETF network slice service.

The RFC also shows how the L3SM and L3NM fit the ACTN framework (RFC 8453): the L3SM between the Customer Network Controller and the Multi-Domain Service Coordinator, and the L3NM between orchestration components such as a parent and a child MDSC.
sections.eli5: Think of a restaurant. The waiter takes the order, the head chef plans the work, and station cooks do the cooking. Each level uses its own kind of instructions.

sections.title: Relationship to Other Models and Sample Uses
sections.content:
The L3NM is not a customer service model and not a device model. The internal view it provides may be mapped to the external L3SM view, but using the L3NM inside a provider neither assumes nor precludes exposing the L3SM. Topology can be represented with the network topology module in RFC 8345. Once a VPN is captured in the L3NM, activation involves device modules such as those for routing management, BGP, PIM, NAT, QoS and ACLs. How the L3NM is used to derive device-specific actions is implementation specific.

Early versions of the L3NM reused data nodes from the L3SM. That was abandoned in favor of the common module in RFC 9181, because it looked as if the L3NM depended on the L3SM.

Three sample uses are given: enterprise L3VPN provisioning and maintenance (adding or removing VPN nodes), multi-domain resource management (route targets and route distinguishers must be coordinated so that two management systems do not export the same RD and prefixes from different PEs), and management of multicast services. For multicast, MP-BGP based MVPNs are the base model taken, since the older dual PIM approach has limitations such as control plane scalability and the need to maintain state in the backbone.
sections.eli5: When two kitchens share one order, they must agree on the ticket numbers, or two dishes could end up with the same number. The model gives them a shared way to write those numbers.

sections.title: Structure: Profiles, Services and Instance Profiles
sections.content:
The ietf-l3vpn-ntw module has two main containers. vpn-profiles holds provider-defined profile identifiers (external connectivity, encryption, QoS, BFD, forwarding and routing) that VPN services can refer to; the model only carries identifiers, and the profiles themselves are local to each provider. vpn-services holds a list of vpn-service entries, each uniquely identified by a vpn-id that is only locally meaningful.

Each service has a name, description, customer name, an optional parent-service-id that ties it back to the order that triggered it (for example an L3SM, network slice or VPN+ request), a VPN type (typically BGP/MPLS L3VPN), a topology (hub-spoke, any-to-any or custom), administrative and operational status, an underlay transport preference and a pointer to external connectivity. A mismatch between administrative and operational status can signal that provisioning actions are needed.

VPN instance profiles factor out settings reused at several levels: the role (such as hub or spoke), local AS, route distinguisher mode, per-address-family route targets and maximum routes, and multicast. They are defined at service level and activated at node and access level. Where the same data node is set at several levels, values at node level override service level, and for access-level data such as multicast, adjusted values override inherited ones. Address families can be ipv4, ipv6 or dual-stack; using dual-stack is RECOMMENDED when values are the same, and dual-stack takes precedence if a node is present for both.
sections.eli5: A profile is a recipe card that lots of dishes can share. A dish can add its own note on the card, and the note wins over the card.

sections.title: VPN Nodes and Network Accesses
sections.content:
A VPN node is an abstraction for the set of policies applied on a network node, typically a PE, for one VPN service. If its ne-id points to a specific PE it will likely map to a VRF instance; it may also point to an abstract node, in which case the network controller decides how to split it into VRF instances. A node can also carry local AS, router IDs per address family, active VPN instance profiles, an optional MSDP configuration for redundancy among rendezvous points, groups, and status.

Each node holds VPN network accesses: the points where customer sites attach, meaning the PE side of the PE-CE connection. Unlike the L3SM, the L3NM does not model the customer site itself. An access has an interface, a type (point-to-point, multipoint, irb or loopback), a reference to an active instance profile, and these containers:

  • connection: Layer 2 details such as dot1q or QinQ encapsulation, Layer 2 tunnels, an L2VPN link for IRB, and an optional LAG interface.
  • ip-connection: IPv4 and IPv6 addressing, with provider DHCP, DHCP relay or static addressing. IPv6 can also use SLAAC.
  • routing-protocols: CE-PE routing, covered below.
  • oam: only BFD is supported in this version.
  • security: encryption, or a local encryption profile.
  • service: bandwidth in bits per second in each direction, MTU, QoS, carriers' carrier, NTP and multicast.

Bearers (the Layer 2 connection to a site) are assumed to be allocated by the provider at service orchestration time, so the model keeps only a bearer-reference to link back to the service request.
sections.eli5: A node is one switchboard in the provider's building for one customer's network. An access is a single plug on that switchboard where the customer's cable goes in.

sections.title: CE-PE Routing Protocols
sections.content:
Each access can have several routing-protocol entries, each with a unique id and a type taken from the common module. The supported protocols are static routing, BGP, OSPF, IS-IS, RIP and VRRP. Several instances of the same protocol are allowed on a link, but that does not force parallel processes on the device. For several BGP peers, a device might run multiple BGP processes with one neighbor each, one process with many neighbors, or a mix; that choice is up to the implementation.

The model deliberately omits low-level routing policy. A service provider's local policies such as filtering belong at the device configuration level, and the model only allows local routing profiles to be associated with an instance. The BGP container is not meant to include every BGP parameter. It covers the neighbor and per-service settings: peer AS, local address, as-override and allow-own-as behavior, maximum prefixes, timers and authentication using TCP-AO, MD5, explicit keys or IPsec.
sections.eli5: The model says which road signs the customer and provider will use to talk to each other, but leaves the detailed traffic rules to the people who run each router.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module is accessed through NETCONF or RESTCONF, with SSH and TLS as the mandatory secure transports, and NACM can restrict access. Many data nodes are writable, and unauthorized writes or deletes could harm the network. Two subtrees are called out as sensitive: vpn-profiles (an attacker might manipulate routing, QoS or encryption policies, and these are tagged default-deny-write) and vpn-services (an attacker could delete a running service, change QoS, bandwidth, routing or keying material, causing SLA violations, or create a service or a network access). Monitoring configuration changes helps detect this.

Readable nodes can be sensitive too: customer-name and ip-connection expose privacy-related information, and keying-material could let an attacker inject spoofed routing advertisements. The authentication nodes rely on RFC 8177 and inherit its security considerations. The module supports MD5 mainly to accommodate the installed BGP base, and the RFC points to the weaknesses of MD5 discussed in RFC 6151 and RFC 6952. For NTP in VPNs it refers to RFC 8633 and RFC 8915.
sections.eli5: Because this model can change how a customer's network works, only trusted people should be able to edit it, and secret keys must not be shown to everyone.

sections.title: Worked Examples in the Appendix
sections.content: Appendix A gives JSON examples. They include a 4G VPN provisioning example, in which an eNodeB acting as the CE connects to a PE over two VLANs and a single vpn-node is created with two network accesses, a loopback interface example, an example of overriding VPN instance profile parameters at node level, and a multicast VPN provisioning example.
sections.eli5: The appendix shows filled-in forms, like a sample homework answer, so you can see what a real request looks like.
